The estimator is the standard random rank-one sketch BBᵀ≈(Bξ)(Bξ)ᵀ applied to a Fisher square-root factor, while the deterministic results mostly follow from elementary properties of diag(p)−ppᵀ. Relevant randomized diagonal/sketching methods and the one-pass sampled-label construction are not adequately discussed.

There are additional technical and presentation errors. For example, the scalar Monte Carlo estimator (1/(4m))∑x_i² has variance Var(x²)/(16m), not Var(x²)/(4m) as stated, and the claim that RelMAE 0.2 means “±20% deviation” is not statistically justified. Overall, the valid core idea is insufficient to overcome the central comparison, soundness, and evaluation problems.

strengths: The paper gives a coherent core-space-to-parameter-space treatment of classifier Fisher matrices, combining simplex spectral analysis, Löwner bounds, and pullbacks through the logit Jacobian.

The proposed random score-gradient construction is simple and practically appealing: it is unbiased, needs one backward pass, and has a clear per-coordinate variance bound for Gaussian and Rademacher probes.
Most formal results are accompanied by proofs, and the low-rank and diagonal variants expose useful accuracy-computation trade-offs.
The empirical study is unusually broad, covering six NLP, vision, and audio settings and comparing against exact diagonal Fisher values on a substantial fixed subset.
weaknesses: The novelty is insufficiently established. The estimator is essentially a randomized Gram-matrix sketch, while closely related one-pass pseudo-label Monte Carlo, randomized per-example-gradient, DiagGGN/Fisher, and vectorized-gradient methods are not adequately discussed or compared.

The computational comparison is questionable: the empirical Fisher is defined as a sum of per-example outer products but is treated as a one-backward-pass baseline without explaining how it is computed. Conversely, the claim that Monte Carlo Fisher requires one backward pass per example overlooks that independently sampled pseudo-label scores can be summed and differentiated in one pass to obtain an unbiased batch-level estimate.

Several theoretical interpretations overreach. The rank-one lower bound and diagonal upper bound are maximal/minimal elements, not respectively a greatest lower bound and least upper bound as claimed. The low-rank lower approximation is also not generally tighter than the diagonal upper approximation; for uniform class probabilities the opposite can hold by a large factor.

The quality guarantee concerns individual diagonal entries and permits a coefficient of variation as large as sqrt(2). A single full-matrix estimate is rank one, yet no matrix-norm concentration or evidence supports the broader claims about accurately estimating the full metric tensor.

The experiments report apparently single random realizations without error bars, probe-count or batch-size ablations, absolute runtimes, memory costs, or sensitivity analyses. RelMAE is highly sensitive to near-zero Fisher entries, and no complementary metric, full-matrix evaluation, or downstream application is provided.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code release, and checkpoint identities, preprocessing, random seeds, training details, and implementation details for the exact and baseline estimators are underspecified. There is also a minor error in the motivating Monte Carlo example, where the variance prefactor should be 1/(16m), not 1/(4m).

The random-projection estimator is simple to implement, unbiased in expectation, requires one reverse-mode pass, and has a useful per-coordinate variance bound for the diagonal Fisher.
The empirical study spans six NLP, vision, and audio configurations, uses expensive exact diagonal-Fisher calculations as ground truth, and reports both approximation error and runtime.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and it explicitly acknowledges the absence of downstream validation.
weaknesses: The central estimator has inadequately established novelty. It is the generic identity E[(Bξ)(Bξ)^T]=BB^T applied to a Fisher/GGN factor and appears equivalent to established stochastic diagonal-GGN or curvature-backpropagation estimators, including machinery associated with BackPACK. The paper cites this literature without clearly distinguishing its method technically.

The most important baseline is excluded on an unconvincing computational premise. A Monte Carlo Fisher using one sampled pseudo-label per example can use the same batched per-example-gradient machinery as the reported one-pass empirical Fisher; an aggregate-score sketch also needs only one backward pass. Claiming that MC necessarily requires B serial backward passes makes the accuracy and efficiency comparison incomplete and potentially unfair.

The evidence supports only diagonal estimation, not the paper's broader claims about estimating the full metric tensor. A single realization is rank one, off-diagonal error is neither analyzed adequately nor evaluated, and there is no downstream optimizer, pruning, or uncertainty application demonstrating utility.

The evaluation lacks repeated-probe statistics or confidence intervals and relies almost entirely on entrywise RelMAE with an epsilon denominator, which can be dominated by the many zero or near-zero Fisher entries visible in the paper. It also does not test the tightness of the deterministic bounds, and several models use random classification heads rather than realistic trained systems.

There are concrete technical inconsistencies. In Section 4.1, for F-hat=(1/(4m)) sum_i x_i^2, the stated variance prefactor should be 1/(16m), not 1/(4m). The heavy-tail example also changes the original fixed-dataset setting into random input sampling, so it is not an apples-to-apples argument against label-sampling MC.

Equation (8) writes one probe ξ_x shared across the k retained eigencomponents, which would introduce cross terms and bias the k>1 estimator; independence would require ξ_{x,i}. The text claims k|D_x| probes, but only the k=1 case is proved, leaving the reported LR(2) method formally ambiguous.

Several conclusions are overstated. In particular, the low-rank lower approximation is not tighter "in general"—near-uniform predictions favor the diagonal upper approximation, as the paper's own random-head experiments show. Likewise, the bounded-relative-standard-deviation result applies to diagonal entries, not the full matrix.

Reproducibility is below top-tier expectations: there is no code, random seeds, precise checkpoint and fine-tuning information, detailed estimator implementation, per-method memory usage, or absolute timing measurements. These omissions are especially consequential given the disputed backward-pass accounting.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent progression from the categorical-simplex Fisher matrix to deterministic neural-network bounds and stochastic estimators. Most derivations are self-contained, with extensive proofs in the appendix.

The randomized construction is simple and potentially useful: it produces an unbiased estimator using one reverse-mode pass per minibatch, and the diagonal variance formulas clearly motivate Rademacher rather than Gaussian probes.

The evaluation covers six model-task settings across language, vision, and speech, using exact diagonal-Fisher targets over 8,192 examples. The proposed estimator achieves consistently encouraging RelMAE values of approximately 0.11–0.22, while low-rank variants perform especially well on some fine-tuned models.
The manuscript is well organized and visually polished, and it explicitly acknowledges the absence of a downstream application.
weaknesses: The main randomized estimator has insufficiently established novelty. Writing the Fisher matrix as AA^T and estimating it by Aξξ^TA^T is a direct random-projection construction closely related to established Monte Carlo generalized-Gauss–Newton, curvature-propagation, and BackPACK-style diagonal-GGN estimators. BackPACK is cited but the apparent equivalence is neither discussed nor experimentally compared, while many deterministic bounds are straightforward consequences of spectral truncation, interlacing, and pullback monotonicity.

The central “envelope” interpretation is mathematically incorrect. Lemma 2 proves only that the proposed bounds are maximal/minimal under a restricted comparability condition, not that they are greatest/least elements in the Loewner order. For example, with p=(1/2,1/2), D=diag(3/8,3/4) is a diagonal upper bound on the simplex Fisher matrix, but diag(p) is not below D; hence diag(p) is not the least diagonal upper bound. Analogously, other eigendirection rank-one lower bounds are incomparable with the leading-eigenvector bound.

Claims of a full metric-tensor estimator with “guaranteed quality” substantially exceed the evidence. The relative-variance guarantee applies only entrywise to the diagonal. A single sample is rank one, no operator- or Frobenius-norm approximation guarantee is given, off-diagonal relative error can be unbounded when the true entry is near zero, and the suggested moving average across changing parameters is not analyzed.

The experimental comparison is incomplete. Standard Monte Carlo is excluded using the assertion that it requires B backward passes, without considering vectorized per-example gradients or established exact/Monte Carlo diagonal-GGN implementations. Moreover, it is unclear how the defined empirical Fisher—an outer-product sum of per-example gradients—is obtained with one ordinary backward pass; squaring the aggregate minibatch gradient would instead introduce cross terms and define a different baseline.

The stochastic evaluation reports only one aggregate result per task, with no repeated probes, uncertainty intervals, convergence versus probe count, sensitivity to minibatch size, or validation of the theoretical variance. Timing differences are mostly negligible, and there is no downstream optimization, pruning, or continual-learning experiment demonstrating practical benefit.

RelMAE is fragile here because it averages elementwise ratios with an arbitrary 10^-12 denominator while the figures show many zero or extremely small Fisher entries. Interpreting RelMAE 0.2 as “±20% relative deviation” is also unjustified. Layerwise robust statistics and absolute or norm-relative errors are needed.

Several technical and reproducibility issues remain: the scalar Monte Carlo example states a variance factor of 1/(4m), whereas its displayed estimator yields 1/(16m); Eq. (8) uses one ξ_x across eigencomponents even though unbiasedness for k>1 requires independently indexed ξ_{x,i}; and no code, seeds, checkpoint identifiers, preprocessing details, or complete timing protocol are supplied. These issues, combined with the novelty and evaluation concerns, place the work below the top-tier acceptance threshold.
